title: Beginner
summary: Everyday phrasal verbs you will hear and use every day.

lessons.meaning: to stop sleeping
lessons.note: Not separable: wake up. (You can say wake someone up: Wake me up at six.)
examples: I wake up at six every morning.
The noise woke me up.
Please wake up. We are late.
reallife: At a hotel: Could you give me a wake-up call? I need to wake up at five.
At home: Wake up, it is time for school.

mistakes.why: Wake up usually means you stop sleeping. To make someone else wake, use wake + person + up.

dialogue: A: What time do you wake up?
B: Around seven. And you?
A: I wake up at six because I walk to work.
conversation.task: Say when you wake up and what you do next.

lessons.cloze: I usually ___ at half past six.

options: stop sleeping
start working
go to bed
assessment.why: Wake up = stop sleeping.

assessment.prompt: I ___ at seven every day. (wake up)
assessment.why: I + base form.

options: The noise woke me up.
The noise woke up I.
The noise wake up me.
assessment.why: Use the object pronoun me between woke and up.

lessons.usage: wake up early; wake someone up

senses.meaning: to stop sleeping
senses.example: I wake up at six every morning.

lessons.meaning: to leave your bed and start the day
lessons.note: Not separable.
examples: I get up at seven.
She gets up early on Sundays.
He did not get up until noon.
reallife: Morning routine: I get up, brush my teeth and have breakfast.
Parent to child: Get up! You will be late for school.

mistakes.wrong: I wake up and get up at the same time always.
mistakes.right: I wake up at six and get up at ten past six.
mistakes.why: Wake up = stop sleeping. Get up = leave the bed. They can be different times.

dialogue: A: Do you get up early?
B: Yes, I get up at five.
A: Why so early?
B: I like a quiet morning.
conversation.task: Say what time you get up on weekdays and at the weekend.

lessons.cloze: On Sundays I do not ___ until nine.

options: leave your bed
go to bed
sit down
assessment.why: Get up = leave your bed.

assessment.prompt: She ___ at six every day. (get up)
assessment.why: She + gets up.

options: He gets up early.
He get up early.
He gets early up.
assessment.why: He + gets up.

senses.meaning: to leave your bed and start the day
senses.example: I get up at seven.

lessons.meaning: to move from standing to sitting
lessons.note: Not separable.
examples: Please sit down.
We sat down at a table by the window.
Sit down and relax.
reallife: At a restaurant: Please sit down. The waiter will come soon.
In class: Sit down, everyone. The lesson is starting.

mistakes.why: Sit down is the normal way to ask someone to take a seat. Sit alone sounds incomplete.

dialogue: A: Come in. Please sit down.
B: Thank you.
A: Would you like some tea?
conversation.task: Invite a guest to sit down and offer them a drink.

lessons.cloze: You look tired. Please ___.

options: take a seat
stand up
walk out
assessment.why: Sit down = take a seat.
An imperative: base form.

options: stand up
wake up
come in
assessment.why: Stand up is the opposite.

senses.meaning: to move from standing to sitting
senses.example: Please sit down.

lessons.meaning: to rise from sitting to standing
lessons.note: Not separable.
examples: Please stand up.
Everyone stood up when the teacher came in.
He stood up and walked to the door.
reallife: At a ceremony: Please stand up for the national anthem.
On a bus: I stood up to give my seat to an older woman.

mistakes.why: The past of stand is stood.

dialogue: A: Please stand up.
B: Why?
A: The guests are here. Let's greet them.
conversation.task: Say when people usually stand up in your country.

lessons.cloze: When the teacher came in, we all ___.

options: rise to your feet
sit on the floor
go to sleep
assessment.why: Stand up = rise to your feet.

assessment.prompt: Yesterday he ___ and left. (stand up; past)
assessment.why: Past tense: stood up.

options: She stood up quickly.
She standed up quickly.
She stand up quickly.
assessment.why: Stood is the past of stand.

senses.meaning: to rise from sitting to standing
senses.example: Please stand up.

lessons.meaning: to enter a room or building
lessons.note: Not separable.
examples: Please come in.
She came in and sat down.
Come in out of the rain.
reallife: Knocking at a door: Hello, may I come in?
Welcoming a guest: Come in, make yourself at home.

mistakes.why: In is part of the phrasal verb. Do not add another preposition.

dialogue: A: Knock, knock. May I come in?
B: Yes, please come in.
A: Thank you. Sorry I am late.
conversation.task: Ask politely if you can come in to someone's office.

lessons.cloze: The door is open. Please ___.

options: enter
leave
wait outside
assessment.why: Come in = enter.

assessment.prompt: He knocked and then ___. (come in; past)
assessment.why: Past of come is came.

assessment.prompt: Which is the best polite question?
options: May I come in?
Come in me?
I come in?
assessment.why: May I come in? is polite.

senses.meaning: to enter a room or building
senses.example: Please come in.

lessons.meaning: to leave your home to do something, often for fun
lessons.note: Not separable. Also: the lights went out (stopped working).
examples: Let's go out for dinner.
I do not go out on weekdays.
She went out with her friends.
reallife: Making plans: Do you want to go out tonight?
Weather: It is raining, so I will not go out.

mistakes.wrong: I go out from home at eight.
mistakes.right: I leave home at eight. / I go out at eight.
mistakes.why: Go out means to leave home for an activity. For a normal departure, leave is more natural.

dialogue: A: Do you want to go out tonight?
B: Sure. Where shall we go?
A: Let's try the new cafe.
conversation.task: Invite a friend to go out this weekend.

lessons.cloze: We often ___ for a walk after dinner.

options: leave home to do something
stay at home
come back
assessment.why: Go out = leave home to do something.

assessment.prompt: Last night we ___ for dinner. (go out; past)
assessment.why: Past of go is went.

options: Do you want to go out tonight?
Do you want go out tonight?
You want to going out tonight?
assessment.why: Want + to + base verb.

senses.meaning: to leave your home to do something, often for fun
senses.example: Let's go out for dinner.

senses.meaning: to stop working or burning (a light or a fire)
senses.example: The lights went out during the storm.

lessons.meaning: to learn a fact or get information
lessons.note: Usually followed by a fact or a clause: find out the price, find out what time it starts.
examples: I will find out the time.
She found out the truth.
Can you find out if the shop is open?
reallife: At work: I will find out the price and call you back.
With friends: Let's find out who won the match.

mistakes.wrong: I want to find out my keys.
mistakes.right: I want to find my keys.
mistakes.why: Find out is for information. For things you lose, use find.

dialogue: A: What time does the train leave?
B: I do not know. I will find out.
A: Thanks. Please text me.
conversation.task: Say what you want to find out about a place you will visit.

lessons.cloze: I need to ___ what time the bank opens.

options: learn information
lose something
look for a place
assessment.why: Find out = learn information.

assessment.prompt: She ___ the answer yesterday. (find out; past)
assessment.why: Past of find is found.

options: I found out that he was ill.
I found out my phone.
I found out under the bed.
assessment.why: Find out + information.

senses.meaning: to learn a fact or get information
senses.example: I will find out the time.

lessons.meaning: to try to find someone or something
lessons.note: Not separable.
examples: I am looking for my keys.
She is looking for a new flat.
What are you looking for?
reallife: In a shop: I am looking for a blue jacket.
At the station: We are looking for platform four.

mistakes.right: I am looking for my phone.
mistakes.why: To search for something, use look for.

dialogue: A: What are you looking for?
B: My glasses. Have you seen them?
A: Yes, they are on the table.
conversation.task: Say what you are looking for at the moment.

lessons.cloze: I am ___ a good restaurant nearby.

options: try to find
see by chance
look after
assessment.why: Look for = try to find.
Present continuous: looking for.

options: She is looking for a job.
She is looking a job.
She is looking at a job for.
assessment.why: Look for + noun.

senses.meaning: to try to find someone or something
senses.example: I am looking for my keys.

lessons.meaning: to lift something, or to collect someone or something
lessons.note: Separable: pick up the bag / pick the bag up / pick it up (never pick up it).
examples: Please pick up your shoes.
I will pick you up at six.
She picked the phone up.
reallife: Family: Can you pick the children up from school?
At a cafe: I will pick up the coffees.

mistakes.why: With a pronoun, put the pronoun between pick and up.

dialogue: A: Can you pick me up from the station?
B: Of course. What time?
A: At eight.
conversation.task: Ask someone to pick you up and say where and when.

lessons.cloze: Could you ___ some milk on your way home?

assessment.prompt: What does 'pick up' mean in 'I will pick you up at six'?
options: collect you
carry you
drop you
assessment.why: Pick up = collect someone.

options: Pick it up.
Pick up it.
Up pick it.
assessment.why: A pronoun goes between pick and up.

assessment.prompt: She ___ her bag and left. (pick up; past)
assessment.why: Past: picked up.

lessons.usage: pick up a friend from the airport

senses.meaning: to lift something, or to collect someone or something
senses.example: Please pick up your shoes.

senses.meaning: to learn a skill or a language without much effort
senses.example: She picked up some Kannada while she lived in Mysuru.

lessons.meaning: to place something on a surface after holding it
lessons.note: Separable: put down the cup / put the cup down / put it down.
examples: Put the box down, please.
He put down his bag and sat.
She put the baby down gently.
reallife: In a shop: Please put down the item if you do not want it.
At home: Put your phone down and listen.

mistakes.why: A pronoun goes between put and down.

dialogue: A: This bag is heavy.
B: Put it down here.
A: Thanks. That is better.
conversation.task: Tell someone to put something down and say where.

lessons.cloze: Please ___ the knife. It is dangerous.

options: place on a surface
pick up
throw away
assessment.why: Put down = place on a surface.

options: Put it down.
Put down it.
Down put it.
assessment.why: A pronoun goes in the middle.

assessment.prompt: He ___ the heavy bag. (put down; past)
assessment.why: The past of put is put.

senses.meaning: to place something on a surface after holding it
senses.example: Put the box down, please.

lessons.meaning: to start a machine or light, so that it works
lessons.note: Separable: turn on the light / turn it on. With a pronoun, the pronoun goes in the middle.
examples: Please turn on the light.
Can you turn the TV on?
It is dark. Turn it on.
reallife: At home: Turn on the fan, it is hot in here.
In a car: Can you turn on the air conditioning?

mistakes.why: With a pronoun (it, them), put the pronoun between turn and on.

dialogue: A: It is dark in here.
B: I will turn on the light.
A: Thank you.
conversation.task: Say what you turn on when you get home.

lessons.cloze: It is dark, so please ___ the light.

options: to do something faster because there is not much time
to start a machine or light, so that it works
to put on clothes or shoes to see if they fit and look good
assessment.why: turn on = to start a machine or light, so that it works.

assessment.prompt: It is dark, so please ___ the light. (turn on)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'turn on'.

options: Turn it on, please.
Turn on it, please.
assessment.why: With a pronoun (it, them), put the pronoun between turn and on.

senses.meaning: to start a machine or light, so that it works
senses.example: Please turn on the light.

lessons.meaning: to stop a machine or light, so that it does not work
lessons.note: Separable: turn off the TV / turn it off.
examples: Please turn off your phone in the cinema.
He turned the light off and went to sleep.
Do not forget to turn the oven off.
reallife: At work: Please turn off the computer before you leave.
At the cinema: Please turn off your mobile phones.

mistakes.why: With a pronoun, put it between turn and off.

dialogue: A: The music is too loud.
B: Sorry, I will turn it off.
A: Thanks.
conversation.task: Say three things you turn off before you go to bed.

lessons.cloze: Please ___ the lights when you leave the room.

options: to make a place tidy and clean
to enter a room or building
to stop a machine or light, so that it does not work
assessment.why: turn off = to stop a machine or light, so that it does not work.

assessment.prompt: Please ___ the lights when you leave the room. (turn off)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'turn off'.

options: Turn off it, please.
Turn it off, please.
assessment.why: With a pronoun, put it between turn and off.

senses.meaning: to stop a machine or light, so that it does not work
senses.example: Please turn off your phone in the cinema.

lessons.meaning: to dress yourself in clothes, shoes or glasses
lessons.note: Separable: put on a coat / put it on.
examples: It is cold. Put on your coat.
She put her shoes on and left.
I put on my glasses to read.
reallife: In winter: Put on a warm hat before you go out.
At the pool: Put on your swimming cap.

mistakes.wrong: Put on it, it is cold.
mistakes.right: Put it on, it is cold.
mistakes.why: With a pronoun (it, them), put the pronoun between put and on.

dialogue: A: It is raining outside.
B: Then put on your raincoat.
A: Good idea.
conversation.task: Say what you put on when it is cold.

lessons.cloze: It is cold outside, so ___ your coat.

options: to dress yourself in clothes, shoes or glasses
to rise from sitting to standing
to stop a machine or light, so that it does not work
assessment.why: put on = to dress yourself in clothes, shoes or glasses.

assessment.prompt: It is cold outside, so ___ your coat. (put on)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'put on'.

options: Put it on, it is cold.
Put on it, it is cold.
assessment.why: With a pronoun (it, them), put the pronoun between put and on.

senses.meaning: to dress yourself in clothes, shoes or glasses
senses.example: It is cold. Put on your coat.

lessons.meaning: to remove clothes or shoes from your body
lessons.note: Separable for clothes: take off your shoes / take them off. For planes: The plane takes off (no object).
examples: Please take off your shoes at the door.
He took his hat off.
The plane takes off at nine.
reallife: At a temple: Please take off your shoes.
At the airport: The plane will take off in ten minutes.

mistakes.why: With a pronoun, put them between take and off.

dialogue: A: Can I come in?
B: Yes, but please take off your shoes.
A: Of course.
conversation.task: Say where you take off your shoes.

lessons.cloze: Please ___ your shoes before you come in.

options: to start a machine or light, so that it works
to remove clothes or shoes from your body
to go more slowly, or to make something go more slowly
assessment.why: take off = to remove clothes or shoes from your body.

assessment.prompt: Please ___ your shoes before you come in. (take off)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'take off'.

options: Take off them, please.
Take them off, please.
assessment.why: With a pronoun, put them between take and off.

senses.meaning: to remove clothes or shoes from your body
senses.example: Please take off your shoes at the door.

senses.meaning: (of a plane) to leave the ground and start to fly
senses.example: The plane takes off at nine.

lessons.meaning: to return to a place where you were before
lessons.note: Not separable: come back (no object).
examples: Please come back at five o'clock.
When will you come back from your trip?
I will come back soon.
reallife: At work: I am going to lunch. I will come back in an hour.
On the phone: Can you come back to me tomorrow?

mistakes.why: Do not use to before home. Say come back home.

dialogue: A: Where are you going?
B: To the shop. I will come back soon.
A: OK, see you later.
conversation.task: Say when you will come back home today.

lessons.cloze: He went to the shop and will ___ in ten minutes.

options: to do something faster because there is not much time
to put on clothes or shoes to see if they fit and look good
to return to a place where you were before
assessment.why: come back = to return to a place where you were before.

assessment.prompt: He went to the shop and will ___ in ten minutes. (come back)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'come back'.

options: Come back home at six.
Come back to home at six.
assessment.why: Do not use to before home. Say come back home.

senses.meaning: to return to a place where you were before
senses.example: Please come back at five o'clock.

lessons.meaning: to return to a place
lessons.note: Not separable: go back (no object).
examples: I want to go back to my country next year.
It is late. Let us go back home.
She went back to work after lunch.
reallife: On holiday: We love this beach. We want to go back next year.
After lunch: It is two o'clock. I must go back to the office.

mistakes.wrong: I will go back to home.
mistakes.why: Do not say to home. Say go home or go back home.

dialogue: A: Are you tired?
B: Yes, let us go back to the hotel.
A: OK, let us go.
conversation.task: Say a place you want to go back to.

lessons.cloze: The lunch break is over, so I must ___ to work.

options: to return to a place
to make a place tidy and clean
to enter a room or building
assessment.why: go back = to return to a place.

assessment.prompt: The lunch break is over, so I must ___ to work. (go back)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'go back'.

options: I will go back to home.
I will go back home.
assessment.why: Do not say to home. Say go home or go back home.

senses.meaning: to return to a place
senses.example: I want to go back to my country next year.

lessons.meaning: to enter a bus, train, plane or ship; or to climb onto a bicycle or horse
lessons.note: Not separable: get on the bus.
examples: Get on the bus at the next stop.
They got on the train at Central Station.
She got on her bicycle and left.
reallife: At a bus stop: We get on the bus at the school.
At the airport: Please get on the plane now.

mistakes.wrong: I get in the bus every day.
mistakes.right: I get on the bus every day.
mistakes.why: Use get on for buses, trains and planes. Use get in for cars and taxis.

dialogue: A: Which bus do I take?
B: Get on number 12.
A: Thank you.
conversation.task: Say where you get on the bus or train.

lessons.cloze: I wait here and ___ the bus at eight.

options: to rise from sitting to standing
to enter a bus, train, plane or ship; or to climb onto a bicycle or horse
to stop a machine or light, so that it does not work
assessment.why: get on = to enter a bus, train, plane or ship; or to climb onto a bicycle or horse.

assessment.prompt: I wait here and ___ the bus at eight. (get on)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'get on'.

options: I get on the bus every day.
I get in the bus every day.
assessment.why: Use get on for buses, trains and planes. Use get in for cars and taxis.

senses.meaning: to enter a bus, train, plane or ship; or to climb onto a bicycle or horse
senses.example: Get on the bus at the next stop.

lessons.meaning: to leave a bus, train, plane, bicycle or horse
lessons.note: Not separable: get off the bus.
examples: Get off at the next stop.
I get off the train at Central Station.
He got off his bike and walked.
reallife: On the bus: Excuse me, I need to get off here.
On a train: This is my stop. I get off here.

mistakes.wrong: I get out of the bus here.
mistakes.right: I get off the bus here.
mistakes.why: Use get off for buses, trains and planes. Use get out of for cars and taxis.

dialogue: A: Where do you get off?
B: At the market.
A: That is the next stop.
conversation.task: Say where you get off the bus or train every day.

lessons.cloze: My stop is next. I need to ___ the bus.

options: to start a machine or light, so that it works
to go more slowly, or to make something go more slowly
to leave a bus, train, plane, bicycle or horse
assessment.why: get off = to leave a bus, train, plane, bicycle or horse.

assessment.prompt: My stop is next. I need to ___ the bus. (get off)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'get off'.

options: I get out of the bus here.
I get off the bus here.
assessment.why: Use get off for buses, trains and planes. Use get out of for cars and taxis.

senses.meaning: to leave a bus, train, plane, bicycle or horse
senses.example: Get off at the next stop.

lessons.meaning: to do something faster because there is not much time

We must hurry up. We are late.
Please hurry up and finish your breakfast.
reallife: At home in the morning: Hurry up, or we will be late for school.

lessons.cloze: The film starts at eight, so please ___.

options: to do something faster because there is not much time
to leave a bus, train, plane, bicycle or horse
to put on clothes or shoes to see if they fit and look good
assessment.why: hurry up = to do something faster because there is not much time.

assessment.prompt: The film starts at eight, so please ___. (hurry up)
assessment.why: Use the phrasal verb 'hurry up'.

options: Hurry up, please.

assessment.why: Hurry up has no object. Do not put it after the verb.

senses.meaning: to do something faster because there is not much time

In a class: Please slow down. I need to write this.

options: to make a place tidy and clean

assessment.why: slow down = to go more slowly, or to make something go more slowly.

senses.meaning: to go more slowly, or to make something go more slowly

Write it down so you do not forget.

options: to rise from sitting to standing
